newsitem.title: UK: Explorer and writer Laurens van der Post dies.
newsitem.headline: Explorer and writer Laurens van der Post dies.

text.p: Sir Laurens van der Post, the South African-born explorer, writer and conservationist, has died aged 90, his daughter said on Monday.

Lucia Crichton-Miller said her father had died peacefully at his London home on Sunday night, just two days he had been due to celebrate his 90th birthday with heir to the throne Prince Charles. The party was cancelled at the last moment because van der Post had fallen ill.
Van der Post earned a world-wide reputation as an explorer and writer, particularly about Africa, in the 1950s but was famous in recent years for being Prince Charles's so-called spiritual guru.
He was godfather to William, the eldest son of Charles and his divorced wife Diana, and was reported to have more influence over Charles than any other person.
Born on his parents' farm in Philippolis in South Africa, van der Post was the 13th of 15 children.
He was the only one of the children not to go to university, choosing instead to start work as a journalist. He became the first Afrikaner journalist on the Natal Advertiser in Durban.
His first book, "In A Province", was thought to be the first written by a South African against racial prejudice. It was published in 1934 by British author Virginia Woolf.
He joined the British Army in 1939 and was captured by the Japanese in Java in 1943.
After his release he returned to Africa to write his most famous books, including the Lost World of the Kalahari in 1958.
He wrote 26 books in all and finished the second volume of his autobiography earlier this year.
His discovery of Jung's theory of the collective subconscious, the communality that binds humans across cultural barriers, changed his life.

It also fired Prince Charles's interest in multi-culturalism and gave him a philosophical framework for his ideas, often ridiculed, ranging from farming to the need for modern Britain to embrace religions other than Christianity.
